---
title: "8.3 Methodology and alternatives"
order: 3
---

Line Increase is one model and three rules, applied in a fixed order. A gradient-boosted
model ranks the booked book on `{{< var li.target >}}`; a threshold on its probability, set
once at training, picks the top of that ranking; a ceiling on the scorecard's PD keeps the
offers inside the risk appetite; the amount rules size the increase; and the pricing engine
decides whether the increase earns its capital. An account is offered only if it passes all
four ([8.1](purpose.qmd#li-funnel)). They are described here in the order the code applies
them.

{{< yt S3-c6 >}}

Session 3 walks through the four clauses and the three caps on two accounts, and then the
funnel over the book. The counts on screen — the booked book, the accounts left after the
probability and PD clauses, after a positive amount, and after the ROE test — are the
funnel facts in [8.1](purpose.qmd#li-funnel): {{< var li.funnel.book.n >}},
{{< var li.funnel.pd.n >}}, {{< var li.funnel.amount.n >}} and {{< var li.funnel.roe.n >}}.
The "growth probability" the video names is the model's probability of
`{{< var li.target >}}`, and the "origination PD" is the scorecard's PD on the booked
account. The referred client the video shows receiving an offer of
\${{< var li.video.amount >}}, at an incremental ROE of {{< var li.video.roe >}}, while "high on
the watchlist" is `{{< var li.video.business_id >}}` (adjudication's decision on it at
origination: {{< var adj.li_video.decision >}}): one of the
{{< var li.offers.ews.High.n >}} offers in Early Warning's {{< var li.video.ews_tier >}} tier
(ranked {{< var li.video.ews_rank >}} by Early Warning's probability), but it is not on the
watchlist the portal serves (no offer is), and its only trigger is
`{{< var li.video.triggers >}}`, a rule offers trip by selection
([8.5](performance.qmd#li-ews)). The video's lesson is that a funnel which says no to most of the book is protecting
it; this chapter adds that {{< var li.cohort_gate.n_cannot_fail >}} of the gates that
check the cohort cannot fail on this book, so the restraint is the rules', and the gate does
not test it (finding 1, [8.7](limitations.qmd)).

## The model: LightGBM

A gradient-boosted tree ensemble, fitted on the {{< var li.n_train >}} training accounts
([8.2](data.qmd#li-split)) with fixed hyperparameters and the platform seed:

```python
model = LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31,   # line_increase/src/train.py
                       subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=SEED,
                       n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, categorical_feature=LI_CATEGORICAL)
```

The hyperparameters are constants, not the result of a search; there is no early stopping
and no calibration step. With {{< var li.model.n_estimators >}} trees of up to
{{< var li.model.num_leaves >}} leaves, the model **fits its training rows almost
perfectly**: training AUC {{< var li.train.auc >}}, against {{< var li.auc >}} on the
held-out accounts ([8.5](performance.qmd#li-held-out-vs-whole-book)). The held-out figures
are sound; the gap matters wherever the model scores its own training rows — which is where
the offer threshold is set and most offers are made (finding 2).

### What the model uses {#li-importance}

LightGBM's own importances, from the saved booster:

{{< include ../../_generated/li-importance.md >}}

By gain the top features are the label's observable drivers and their companions: the
balance, revenue and utilisation. Because two inputs restate others
([8.2](data.qmd#li-features)), each driver's credit is split between a pair: utilisation and
`util_headroom` together carry {{< var li.importance.pair_gain_share >}} of the gain, and
`annual_revenue` and `log_revenue` {{< var li.importance.revenue_gain_share >}}. Read as a
ranking of single columns, the table understates both. `pd_score` ranks
{{< var li.importance.gain.pd_score_rank >}}th by gain and
{{< var li.importance.split.pd_score_rank >}}rd by split count. Importance says how the
trees spread their splits, not what the model would lose without a feature; the single-column
baselines in [8.5](performance.qmd#li-baselines) are the better guide.

## The offer threshold, calibrated at training {#li-threshold}

After fitting, `train.py` sets the threshold as a quantile of the model's probability over
**all** {{< var li.n_book >}} booked accounts — training and held-out rows together — and
writes it into `metadata.json`:

```python
prob_full = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]                        # line_increase/src/train.py
threshold = float(round(np.quantile(prob_full, LINE_INCREASE["offer_quantile"]), 4))
```

With `offer_quantile` = {{< var li.config.offer_quantile >}}, the committed threshold is
{{< var li.offer_threshold >}}, and {{< var li.thr.share_book >}} of the book clears it by
construction. Like Early Warning's tier cutoffs ([D7.3](../ews/methodology.qmd#ews-tiers)),
the threshold fixes a **share of the book**, not a probability: on a retrain it moves to keep
the share. Because {{< var li.n_train >}} of the {{< var li.n_book >}} probabilities it is
taken over are in-sample, it is set partly on probabilities the model has memorised; on this
model the effect on the share is small — {{< var li.thr.share_holdout >}} of held-out accounts
clear it, against {{< var li.thr.share_train >}} of training rows — but every offer is chosen
from the same in-sample ranking (finding 2).

## The risk-appetite ceiling {#li-pd-ceiling}

The same run sets a ceiling on the scorecard's PD:

```python
max_pd = float(round(np.quantile(pd_score, LINE_INCREASE["max_pd_quantile"]), 4))   # train.py
```

With `max_pd_quantile` = {{< var li.config.max_pd_quantile >}}, the ceiling,
{{< var li.offer_max_pd >}}, is the book's median PD: the module offers only to the
lower-risk half of the book. It is a policy choice expressed as a quantile, so it too keeps a
share of the book and not a level of risk. It is not fitted to the label, and it excludes
every account in score band D, whose lowest PD is {{< var li.band.D.pd_min >}}
([8.5](performance.qmd#li-bands)).

## The amount rules {#li-amount}

`recommended_amount` (`line_increase/src/amount_rules.py`) takes the lowest of three caps:

```python
target_limit = current_balance / cfg["target_util"]              # amount_rules.py
raw_delta = target_limit - credit_limit
pct_cap = cfg["pct_cap"] * credit_limit
revenue_ceiling = cfg["revenue_mult_cap"] * annual_revenue - credit_limit
delta = min(raw_delta, pct_cap, revenue_ceiling)
if delta <= 0:
    return 0.0
rnd = cfg["round_to"]
return float(round(delta / rnd) * rnd)
```

| Cap | Setting (`shared.config.LINE_INCREASE`) | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Headroom to target utilisation | `target_util` = {{< var li.config.target_util >}} | raise the limit until today's balance uses only this share of it |
| Share of the current limit | `pct_cap` = {{< var li.config.pct_cap >}} | never raise the limit by more than this share at once |
| Revenue ceiling | `revenue_mult_cap` = {{< var li.config.revenue_mult_cap >}} | the new limit stays within this multiple of annual revenue |

The amount is rounded to `round_to` = {{< var li.config.round_to >}}. The first cap is
positive only when utilisation is above `target_util`, so **an amount requires a constrained
account**: every account with one has utilisation of at least
{{< var li.cohort_gate.util.min_amount >}}. Which cap binds, on the lowest of the three
(`app/v2/li_amounts.py`, the first on a tie):

{{< include ../../_generated/li-caps.md >}}

Every cap binds somewhere: the count of caps that bind on no account with an amount is
{{< var li.caps.n_dead >}}. Most of the book has no headroom at all: on {{< var li.caps.no_headroom >}} accounts
the lowest cap is at or below zero, and on {{< var li.caps.rounds_to_zero >}} more a positive
cap rounds to zero. The revenue ceiling is at or below zero on
{{< var li.caps.revenue_negative >}} accounts, whose limit already exceeds
`revenue_mult_cap` times their revenue.

## The incremental ROE test {#li-roe}

The increase is priced by the pricing engine, not by this module:

```python
def incremental_exposure(delta_amount, utilization_onbook):       # amount_rules.py
    """EAD of the incremental limit: drawn at current on-book utilization (clipped 0-1)."""
    util = min(max(float(utilization_onbook), 0.0), 1.0)
    return float(delta_amount) * util
...
    ead = incremental_exposure(delta_amount, utilization_onbook)
    w = waterfall_or_zero(pd_, ead, rate, market)
    return {
        "incremental_ead": ead,
        "roe": w["roe"],
        "clears_hurdle": bool(ead > 0 and w["roe"] >= market.roe_hurdle),
```

The increment is assumed drawn at the account's current utilisation
([8.4](assumptions.qmd#li-drawdown)), and priced with `profit_waterfall` at the scorecard's PD
and the account's own quoted rate, against `MARKET`'s hurdle of
{{< var li.gate.roe_hurdle >}}. Two properties follow from D6's engine:

- **The ROE does not depend on the size of the increase.** Every line of the waterfall is
  proportional to EAD, so the ROE at the incremental EAD equals the ROE at an EAD of one: over
  the offers the largest difference is {{< var li.econ.ead_invariance >}} ([8.4](assumptions.qmd#li-drawdown)).
- **The test is therefore the pricing test on the loan itself.** On all
  {{< var li.econ.pricing_agree >}} accounts with an amount, the increment's verdict equals
  `price_loan`'s verdict on the existing loan at its quoted rate. An account is offered more
  only if its existing loan already clears the hurdle at the rate it pays; D6's findings about
  that verdict arrive here ([D6.7](../pricing/limitations.qmd)).

Of the {{< var li.funnel.amount.n >}} accounts that pass the first three clauses, the ROE test
removes {{< var li.funnel.roe.dropped >}}.

The module's own configuration holds a hurdle too, `LINE_INCREASE["roe_hurdle"]`
({{< var li.config.roe_hurdle >}}). No file in `line_increase/src` reads it: the hurdle that
decides is `MARKET`'s, through `incremental_roe`'s `market` argument
({{< var li.config.n_unread >}} unread key: `{{< var li.config.unread >}}`). Today the two
are equal; finding 4.

## Why a gradient-boosted model {#li-why-lightgbm}

The label's drivers have thresholds (utilisation matters only above a level) and the output
is an offer list for review, not a credit decision, so a flexible learner that finds
thresholds without hand-binning fits the problem, and Tier 2 ([D0](../d0-summary.qmd#risk-tiering))
makes the loss of an exact decomposition tolerable. The choice was made at development and is
recorded here so it can be challenged. What the evidence says, from
[8.5](performance.qmd#li-baselines):

- **It beats every single input.** No single numeric input reaches the AUC gate; the best,
  `{{< var li.baseline.best.feature >}}`, reaches {{< var li.baseline.best.auc >}}, and the
  model's paired lead over it is {{< var li.baseline.revenue.diff_lo >}} to
  {{< var li.baseline.revenue.diff_hi >}}.
- **It sits close to the data's ceiling.** It gets {{< var ceiling.li.share_of_reach >}} of
  the way from a coin toss to the noise-free logit on the same rows
  ([8.5](performance.qmd#li-ceiling)).

### Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Status | What it would and would not give |
|---|---|---|
| Rank by utilisation or revenue alone | measured, not adopted | Both pass the lift gate alone; neither reaches the AUC gate, and the model beats both with paired intervals above zero ([8.5](performance.qmd#li-baselines)). |
| Rank by the scorecard's PD alone | measured, not adopted | A weak ranking for this label ({{< var li.baseline.pd_score.auc >}}): low risk is not the same as a good candidate. |
| A logistic or scorecard-style model | not built | Exact reasons and far less room to memorise the training rows (finding 2); whether it would rank as well is unmeasured. |
| Rules alone: utilisation above `target_util`, PD within appetite, ROE clears | not measured | The three rules already decide most of the funnel; what the model adds to them on outcomes is not measured (finding 1). |

## Reason codes: SHAP

As in adjudication and Early Warning, the reasons come from SHAP: `score_population` runs
`shap.TreeExplainer` over every booked account and keeps each account's top three features
pushing the probability up, with the shared `top_adverse_shap` helper (here the "adverse"
direction is towards an offer). The v2 workbench serves them; the v1 account endpoint does not.
`train.py` runs
the explainer on a few held-out rows as a sanity check only. They carry D5's caveats, and the
redundant pairs split credit between restatements of one driver
([8.2](data.qmd#li-features)).

## Feature selection

None, in the sense of a search: `LI_FEATURE_COLUMNS` is a fixed list. `colsample_bytree`
draws a random subset of columns for each tree, which is regularisation, not selection.
